poiSLA-desc:
Eurasia, despite its unfamiliar name, is the successor state to old Russia. It was created approximately around the advent of the Great Mistake in order to deal with the issues that faced the Russian state at the time. Disproportionate minority rights, {{poiSLA013|an overly powerful oligarchy}} and lack of representation within the state. This decision would send Eurasia on yet another course for disaster.

After {{poiSLA002|a failed invasion of Central Asia}}, the Eurasian Union broke. The old oligarchic families that ruled the old federation were still tasting sour grapes and flung the Union into civil war. Whilst the war has died down, {{poiSLA003|the insurgencies continue}}. {{poiSLA008|The Karelians}} wish to {{poiSLA015|restore the oligarchic system}}, {{poiSLA006|the Siberians}} wish to {{poiSLA012|bring back systems from Russia's past}}, {{poiSLA005|the Uralic Army Group South}} wish to seek power for themselves and {{poiSLA016|the Vostoslavs}} seek to create their own state.

{{poiSLA001|The Eurasians}}, however, seek to create the {{poiSLA004|Slavic Federation}}, a proposed alliance between {{poiSLA017|all of Slavic Europe}} that'd be able to counter the superstates of China, Franco-Iberia and the EAF. This is of course, only a dream, but one that seems closer each and every day.

A riddle, wrapped in a mystery, inside an enigma.
poiSLA001-desc:
The most celebrated cosmonaut since Yuri Gagarin, Vadim Kozlov came from a working-class family but rose to heroic stature in the years following the Dark Age.

Eldest son of parents who labored as itinerant steelworkers and welders, Vadim acquired his limited formal education in industrial cities scattered across the Federation. Inducted into the armed forces and immediately given the rank of Colonel, Vadim took advantage of part-time educational programs to gain a comp-diploma in aerospace engineering. Over the next decade, he became the public face of the Federation efforts to exploit the vast resources of space.

Incredibly popular among the working class, a devoted family man, and fiercely loyal to the Slavic state that had rewarded his hard work, Kozlov eschewed offers to enter politics or move into the civilian realm. Vadim Kozlov is the founder of the Slavic Federation, which he sees as a necessary step towards human progress.
poiSLA002-desc:
Siberia is burning. The Great Mistake has not only flooded the Vorkuta region but wiped entire cities off the map. The Caspian's sudden expansion shattered the Central Asian campaign of 2154, cutting off nation's access to Asia. Entire steppes are catching fire, while warlord remnants continue to harass those who dare venture outside the Core Cities. Restoring Siberia to its former beauty is now an impossible task.

When the Great Mistake grew to encompass Siberia, some thought that the region would benefit. How wrong they were. All across the Siberian landscape, uncontrolled fires are spreading. Rivers have expanded to swallow entire towns. Acid rain has become a common sight. But the sky remains grey.

In the Ural Mountains, simple survival is a challenge. Rampant forest fires, unpredictable floods, and roving marauders make life impossible. Those who could, have already fled. Those who remain, they are the dead. All that remains is the fire of the wasteland.
poiSLA003-desc: The Eurasian Military, composed of the Army, Navy, Air and Space branches, is very young. Most soldiers are veterans of the Dark Ages, and many are still loyal to local warlords. Recent efforts to centralize the military around the Verhuvnaya Commanda—based in the capital—have not been as successful as hoped. It would be naive to believe that the ragged men Eurasians call soldiers have anything but money in mind. All future campaigns should be executed quickly, lest the officers decide to switch loyalties.
poiSLA004-desc:
The Slavic Federation is less of a unitary entity and more of an alliance of convenience. Eurasia, still viewing itself as the protector of junior Slavic peoples, sends out regular relief aid to other members. While a uniting force amongst Slavic nations, conservative elements of society argue for a more aggressive approach towards exerting foreign influence and believe that the Federation is more of a liability than a strength.

Being Kozlov's brainchild, he is unlikely to give it up, but there are rumors of growing discontent amongst its members.
poiSLA005: No Army, No State, No Nothing
poiSLA005-desc:
The Urals are inhabited by the remnants of Army Group South. Originally a grand Eurasian force sent to reinforce the rapidly deteriorating situation in old Kazakhstan, the entire army routed due to a variety of reasons, including poor supply and low morale. The collapse of the campaign led to most of the army retreating past the Urals. The decentralized government in Eurasia failed to rally the deserters, and instead relied upon the League to stem the inflow of Far Eastern refugees.

But for the people of the Urals, there is nothing left. The villages are reduced to ash, the people empty husks. Once proud-soldiers, now reduced to pillaging. What lies ahead, a dense fog.
poiSLA006-desc: Roughly half of Siberia's population consists of migrant Chinese. Local minorities have long been displaced and forgotten, but Russian nationalists dominate the government. Any type of cohesion is impossible as long as either side is hostile to the other.
poiSLA007-desc:
The infamous Luo Zhenxian, or Siberian Brigade, was hastily organized by the old Chinese government during the mass exodus of Northern populations into Siberia. Originally tasked with protecting refugees by working with local Siberian authorities, the brigade's leader, {{poiSLA014|Lei Chang}}, has grown disillusioned with the treatment of refugees in the icy wastes.

The Luo Zhenxian now wages an undercover war against Sibir, and if not stopped in time, may cause the total collapse of Russian authority in the region.
poiSLA008-desc: The old Russian Republic, currently based in Karelia, is the descendant of {{poiSLA011|the failed Republican Revolution of 2156}}. Once encompassing much of Siberia and old Russia, the Revolution has fortified its peninsula in hopes of waiting out the Moscow Regime. But as Eurasia grows stronger by the day, the Russian Republic must strike soon or die.
poiSLA009-desc: The Karelian lands have long been emptied of their namesake population—what is left are squabbling tribes of Slavs and Finnish refugees fleeing from the West. National divisions are high, and although the Republic preaches peace between the two groups, daily brawls and shootouts are not an uncommon sight.
poiSLA010-desc:
Liev Ganin never understood warfare in a technical sense. Having cheated his way through the Suvorov Military Academy, he found himself armed and sent into the meatgrinder of Central Asia. The campaign dragged on for many years, claiming all of Liev's friends.

The Great Rout came at the climax of the campaign in 2157, by which point Liev's skill for improvisation and limited tactical expertise had landed him the undesirable position of general. Following the migration of Army Group South into the Urals, Liev settled in the mountain chain, drinking his sorrows away. However, either semi-consciously or through gritted teeth, Liev Ganin is digging up old hatchets.
poiSLA011-desc:
Far from home, and far from happiness. Boris Morozov is one of the few who still remember the Eurasian Republican Movement, and one of fewer still who took part in it. Its climax came in 2156, when its leaders and followers marched on the capital of Eurasia and the military answered by massacring them. Like many republicans, Morozov fled, lost everything and found himself in Siberia.

He rebuilt his life through politics, though much of his fire had gone out. He remained a political mastermind, and his dedication to democracy and his reform of the aging Siberian parliament eventually made him President of Siberia. Now depression is all that fills him. He sees the coming political storm and knows he is too old to keep fighting. Parliament urges him to choose a successor, but every candidate seems consumed by vanity, and none can be trusted with the republican gem he has worked so hard to cut.
poiSLA012-desc:
Siberia is seen as a relic of past centuries, a reminder of old ideologies and bygone ideals, and it has become a hotbed for politicians who still cling to them. Lyubochka Xun, born to a Chinese immigrant and a Siberian native during the refugee crisis, was one of the luckier newcomers to Siberian society. Half Russian and half Chinese, she carries both in her politics.

An idealist to the extreme, she sees socialism as the only answer to the global crisis. In her eyes, draconian authority and the abandonment of humanitarian and egalitarian ideals were the powder keg that exploded when the Great Mistake set the world alight, and only the collective effort of a unified people can bring real progress. Born of the first nation to raise the red flag and of the nation that carried it into the present, she believes she can be the one to set it in motion. The Revolution does not sleep. You are either with her, or against her.
poiSLA013-desc:
To Saltanov Balakin, the world needs a great correction. Society's current path is unsustainable and misguided, and it needs a leader who will crack down hard on its parasites. The answer is simple: a swift kick to the bourgeoisie, the seizure of their wealth, and a regimented, ordered labour force to carry humanity to new levels of capability, survival and equality.

Born to a middle-class family in Irkutsk, Balakin saw first-hand what an over-capitalised society brings down on humanity, and could only watch as his friends and countrymen failed to escape or recover from the ecological disasters that ravaged his country and the world. Today he sits in the upper ranks of the Siberian Parliament as head of the Sword and Hammer faction of the Siberian Socialist Party, determined to seize any chance to root out corruption and capitalist dogma and remind people what humanity really means.
poiSLA014-desc:
In the chaotic reshuffling of ministers, officials and generals that followed the Great Mistake in China, Colonel Lei Chang rose to command a brigade of the Nuzhen People's Corps that would earn the name {{poiSLA007|Luo Zhenxian}}. Under the Northern Treaty of 2168 with the Siberian government, Chinese settlement was not to cross north of a border drawn along the Olyokma and Vitim rivers. When refugees began flowing again after unrest in Dongbei, the Corps could not help those who had fled further north because of overcrowding, a betrayal Lei despised.

Against the treaty and the wishes of Beijing, he took the Luo Zhenxian across the river to help his abandoned countrymen settle the hostile wilderness. For several years he ran a de facto independent clique from Mogocha in Zabaykalsky, where a stable life took shape between his men and the city. When China rebuilt its central authority, he was declared a warlord, and after a brief conflict he fled with his soldiers north across the settlement line into what is now the Siberian Republic.

Many see the Colonel as a tyrant, at best a preacher of false hope, at worst a dangerous old man. Iron-fisted and zealous as he is, Lei Chang wants nothing more than a China free of demagogues and radicals: a place where his people can live and prosper, where soldiers can go home to their families, and where China can rebuild its heritage and carry it into the future.
poiSLA015-desc:
To another hundred years! The Karelian Duma, self-proclaimed successor to the assembly of the Russian Federation, sits in the desolate far north, cut off from the bulk of the old revolutionary forces in Siberia. Its situation worsens by the day. Constant equipment shortages, corruption, and {{poiSLA009|ethnic tension between Slavs and migrating Finnish tribes}} have taken their toll on the rump state.

Thanks to the Byzantine politics of the Republic, the Duma has no president or acting representative. Every member has a vote and in theory represents a region of old Russia, even if they have never set foot there. Decisions are possible only because of a shared hatred of Eurasia, which waits across the lake for Karelia to starve. The Duma has other plans.
poiSLA016-desc:
Ever since old Belarus was incorporated into Russia after the Great Mistake, the Vostoslavic peoples have lived under the Eurasian yoke. An unruly blend of Belarusian, Russian, Ukrainian, Polish, German, Baltic and other nationalities, the Vostoslavs have been a thorn in Moscow's side for years, never fully accepting integration but declining every provocation to a futile revolt.

Eurasia, beset by economic problems and bogged down in its eastern quagmires, has never managed to impose its national identity on them. Its efforts, mostly reworked school curriculums and, for a short while, mandatory adult re-education classes, only fed regional nationalism. Radical Vostoslavs, inspired by figures such as Maxim Veliki and Oscar Sambuk, have instead embraced their own pan-Slavism, and the garrisons in Minsk grow more nervous every year.
poiSLA017-desc: Ukraine is home to many Slavic peoples. Beside Ukrainians and Russians, Belarusians, Vostoslavs, Poles and others have sought refuge along the Danube, and sometimes that diversity breeds chaos. The bigger problem lies to the east. Eurasia occupied eastern Ukraine in the late 21st century, and its enterprises have shackled the country ever since: Russian businessmen own its factories, its plantations and even minor army units. Kyiv must either stabilize the relationship, or find someone else to stand beside.
poiSLA018-desc:
For almost forty years, the Balkan Federation's economy has followed the Novite Balkani Plan, drafted by the Bulgarian economist Mila Nankova to maximize growth through consumer spending and high-value specialized goods. Many credit her for the Federation's financial success, and it has not suffered a serious famine since 2137. Since her death in 2189 the plan has been losing favour, and talks are under way to rework it for short-term militarization and industrial automation. Both INTEGR and Eurasian advisors criticize it for its harmful side effects.

The Federation's polarisation is watched across Europe. The green-socialist Communalists, joined by radical anti-capitalists, campaign for care of the Earth through a more centralised and equal economy, and blame capitalism for the Great Mistake. Against them stands the National Sovereignty Coalition, which claims the Communalists are nurtured by Germany and INTEGR to provoke a civil rupture and intervene. The Federation's President, Ivan Vodovich, has to hold the country together between INTEGR and the Slavic Federation.
